title: Exposed MCP Server: From Recon to OAuth Security Flaws
summary_en: The MCP service allowed anyone to register an OAuth client without authentication and without validating the redirect_uri, resulting in an open‑redirect and SSRF that can be used to steal authorization codes.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a missing authentication check on the dynamic client registration endpoint (POST /mcp/register), allowing unauthenticated users to create clients. The server also fails to validate the "redirect_uris" parameter, so any attacker‑controlled URL is accepted. Because the redirect_uri is later used by the authorization endpoint without verification, the service performs an open redirect. Additionally, the backend fetches the supplied URL during registration, causing a server‑side request forgery (SSRF). These flaws stem from trusting user‑provided data without proper sanitisation or access control.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Open the base MCP URL in a browser.
GET https://REDACTED/mcp
Why: An HTTP request (a message sent to a server) returns a simple JSON response showing the service is alive.
Step 2: Run dirsearch (a directory‑brute‑forcing tool) against the host.
GET https://REDACTED/dirsearch_output.txt
Why: The tool enumerates hidden paths; it discovered an "/examples/" directory.
Step 3: Browse the discovered sitemap file.
GET https://REDACTED/examples/sitemap.xml
Why: A sitemap (XML file) often lists internal URLs; it revealed "/examples/api-reference.html".
Step 4: Open the API reference page.
GET https://REDACTED/examples/api-reference.html
Why: The page documents all HTTP endpoints, including the OAuth flow.

DISCOVERY
Step 5: Locate the client‑registration endpoint in the docs.
POST /mcp/register
Why: The documentation shows the HTTP method (POST) and path; this endpoint creates OAuth clients.
Step 6: Note the "redirect_uris" parameter definition (an array of URLs).
Why: A parameter is a piece of data sent to the server; here it tells the auth server where to send users after login.

EXPLOITATION
Step 7: Craft a registration request with a domain you control (Burp Collaborator).
POST /mcp/register HTTP/2
Host: REDACTED
Content-Type: application/json

{"client_name":"My AI App","redirect_uris":["https://COLLABORATOR.example/"]}
Why: This payload (the body of the request) registers a new client; no authentication is required, so anyone can send it.
Step 8: Send the request and receive a 201 Created response.
HTTP/2 201 Created
{"client_id":"REDACTED","client_secret":"REDACTED","redirect_uris":["https://COLLABORATOR.example/"]}
Why: The server accepted the unvalidated redirect_uri and returned credentials.
Step 9: Observe DNS and HTTP interactions on the Collaborator domain.
GET / HTTP/1.1\nHost: COLLABORATOR.example
Why: The server fetched the supplied URL, proving an SSRF (server‑side request forgery) where the backend makes outbound requests to attacker‑controlled hosts.
Step 10: Build an authorization request using the new client_id and redirect_uri.
GET /mcp/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=REDACTED&redirect_uri=https://COLLABORATOR.example/&scope=openid&state=TEST&code_challenge=REDACTED&code_challenge_method=S256
Why: This HTTP GET (request) starts the OAuth flow; the redirect_uri is again unchecked, so the user is sent to the attacker domain.
Step 11: Open the URL in a browser and watch the redirect.
Browser navigates to https://COLLABORATOR.example/?code=...&state=TEST
Why: The open redirect leaks the authorization code to the attacker, enabling token exchange.

IMPACT
Step 12: Use the captured code to request an access token (not shown in article but implied).
POST /mcp/token with code=...&client_id=REDACTED&client_secret=REDACTED
Why: With the code, an attacker can obtain a JWT (JSON Web Token) and act as the victim user.
lesson.example:
Assume a fictional service at https://target.example that offers OAuth client registration at POST /oauth/register. The server code (vulnerable) simply stores the supplied "redirect_uris" array without checks:

```python
# vulnerable snippet
data = json.loads(request.body)
client_id = generate_id()
store[client_id] = {
    "redirect_uris": data.get("redirect_uris", []),
    "secret": generate_secret()
}
return json.dumps({"client_id": client_id, "client_secret": store[client_id]["secret"]})
```
An attacker sends:

POST /oauth/register HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{"client_name":"evil","redirect_uris":["https://attacker.example/cb"]}

The server replies with a new client_id and secret. Later, the attacker initiates:

GET /oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=123&redirect_uri=https://attacker.example/cb&state=xyz

The service redirects the user to https://attacker.example/cb?code=...&state=xyz, leaking the code. Because the redirect_uri was never validated, the attack works. The same flaw also causes the server to request https://attacker.example during registration, demonstrating SSRF.
lesson.takeaway: When you see an unauthenticated client‑registration endpoint, assume the redirect_uri may be unchecked. Look for "redirect_uris" or similar parameters in OAuth docs and test with a domain you control. Tools like Burp Collaborator or dnslog can confirm out‑bound requests (SSRF) and redirects. Variants include open‑redirects in SAML ACS URLs or OpenID Connect "post_logout_redirect_uri". Beginners often forget to check whether the server validates the URL scheme or domain, leading to false‑negative results.

title: Android Deep Link Hijacking to Account Takeover via OAuth Code Interception
summary_en: An attacker can intercept OAuth authorization codes by registering a malicious app with the same custom URI scheme as a legitimate app, leading to full account takeover.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from two main flaws: the use of a non-exclusive custom URI scheme (app-login://) and the storage of sensitive OAuth credentials (client_id and client_secret) inside the publicly accessible APK file (the Android application package). Because Android allows any app to claim a custom URI scheme, a malicious app can 'hijack' the link intended for the real app. Furthermore, because the app's secret keys were hardcoded, the attacker had everything needed to complete the login process once the code was stolen.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher decompiles (turning an app file back into readable code) the APK to read the AndroidManifest.xml (a file in an app that lists its features and permissions).
2. They identify an intent-filter (a setting that tells Android which links an app can open) using a custom URI scheme (the part of a link like app:// that tells the device which app to use).
<data android:scheme="app-login" android:host="m.example.com" />
Why: This tells us the app listens for links starting with app-login:// to handle logins.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher uses JADX (a tool to turn app files into code) to search for the custom scheme and OAuth (a system for sharing data without passwords) secrets.
4. They find a hardcoded client_secret (a password for the app itself) in the Java source code.
private static final String CLIENT_SECRET = "...";
Why: Hardcoded secrets can be read by anyone who downloads the app, as APKs are not encrypted.
EXPLOITATION
5. The researcher creates a malicious PoC (Proof of Concept) app that includes the exact same intent-filter in its own manifest.
6. They install both the legitimate app and the malicious app on the same Android device.
7. The researcher triggers the email verification flow in the legitimate app, which sends a login link to their email.
8. They open the email and click the "Open in App" button.
9. Android displays an app chooser (a menu asking which app to use) because two apps claim the same link.
10. The researcher selects the malicious app from the list.
11. The malicious app receives the intent (a message containing data) which includes the auth_code (a temporary secret used to get a login token).
app-login://m.example.com/?auth_code=...
Why: The sensitive code meant for the real app was successfully diverted to the attacker's app because the scheme was not unique.
12. The malicious app extracts the auth_code using the getQueryParameter method.
String authCode = data.getQueryParameter("auth_code");
Why: This pulls the specific parameter (a piece of information added to a URL) from the intercepted link.
IMPACT
13. The malicious app sends an HTTP POST request (a message sending data to a server) to the token endpoint (a specific web address for authentication).
https://api.example.com/oauth2/token
Why: This exchanges the stolen code and hardcoded secret for an access token (a digital key that proves a user is logged in).
14. The attacker uses the resulting token to request the user's private profile data, proving full account takeover.
https://api.example.com/2.0/users/me
Why: The server believes the attacker is the legitimate user because they provided a valid token.
lesson.example:
Suppose a fictional app 'TargetApp' uses the scheme 'target-auth://' for logins. We assume the app's APK contains a hardcoded secret 'SECRET_999'. An attacker creates 'EvilApp' which also handles 'target-auth://'. When a user clicks a login link like 'target-auth://callback?code=ABC123', they are prompted to choose an app and might pick 'EvilApp'. The attacker's app then sends this request: 

POST /oauth/token HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

code=ABC123&client_id=target_id&client_secret=SECRET_999

The server sees a valid code and the correct secret, so it issues a login token to the attacker, who now controls the user's account.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for Android bugs, always check the AndroidManifest.xml for custom URI schemes in intent-filters. Use tools like JADX to decompile the APK and search for hardcoded strings like 'client_secret' or 'api_key'. A common variant of this bug involves 'App Links' that are improperly configured, allowing hijacking even on modern Android versions. Beginners often forget that APKs are not encrypted; any 'secret' stored inside them is public knowledge. Look for OAuth flows where the redirect_uri uses a custom scheme instead of a verified https domain.
lesson.fix: To fix this, developers must use Android App Links with the 'autoVerify=true' attribute in the manifest. This requires hosting a 'digital-asset-links.json' file on the web server to prove the app owns the domain, preventing other apps from hijacking the links. Additionally, sensitive credentials like the client_secret must never be hardcoded in the app. Instead, use the OAuth PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) extension, which uses a dynamically generated secret for each login session, making intercepted codes useless without the session-specific key.

title: Insecure Authorization on *** Android — mobile application
summary_en: The Android app's exported CustomTabFlowActivity accepts any OAuth/SSO redirect URI without verifying state, nonce, or PKCE, so an attacker can inject a forged redirect and hijack browser-based OAuth flows such as third-party Marketplace (Google Drive) account linking.
summary_ar: في تطبيق Android، الـ Activity المصدّرة CustomTabFlowActivity بتستقبل أي URI redirect من تدفقات OAuth/SSO من غير ما تتحقق من state أو nonce أو PKCE، فالمهاجم يقدر يحقن redirect مزيف ويختطف تدفق OAuth زي ربط تطبيقات Marketplace (Google Drive) ويحصل على صلاحيات غير مصرح بها.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause إن الـ Activity اسمها CustomTabFlowActivity مكتوبة في الـ manifest بـ android:exported="true" ومسجّلة كـ redirect target لعدة تدفقات OAuth/SSO حساسة مبنية على المتصفح، زي com.canva.editor://oauth (مستخدم في ربط تطبيقات Marketplace تبع طرف تالت زي Google Drive) و canva://sso وكمان App Links على canva.com. الباحث فكّك التطبيق وتتبّع مسار معالجة الـ redirect: CustomTabFlowActivity -> CustomTabFlowViewModel.f(Uri) -> BrowserFlowResultManager.a(Uri). في أي نقطة في المسار ده مفيش تحقق إن الـ state أو code أو token اللي جايين في الـ URI مربوطين بتدفق بدأه نفس الـ instance من التطبيق — مفيش مقارنة nonce/state، مفيش فحص PKCE verifier، ومفيش تحقق من هوية الـ caller. النتيجة إن أي URI بيتوصّل للـ Activity بيتعاد نشره كأنه "flow completed" لأي business logic شغّالة في اللحظة دي، من غير أي إثبات إنه فعلاً نتيجة تدفق شرعي.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث كان بيفحص تطبيق Android لهدف bug bounty، وبدأ بمراجعة الـ manifest عشان يلاقي الـ Activities المصدّرة والـ deep links. لفت نظره إن CustomTabFlowActivity مكتوبة بـ android:exported="true" ومسجّلة كـ redirect target لتدفقات OAuth/SSO حساسة: com.canva.editor://oauth (مستخدم في ربط تطبيقات Marketplace تبع طرف تالت زي Google Drive)، com.canva.editor://external-app-config، canva://sso، وكمان App Links على https://www.canva.com/oauth/transfer و /login/sso/transfer و /apps/oauth/authorized/app و /apps/configured/app مع autoVerify="true". عشان يفهم اللي بيحصل فعلاً، فكّك التطبيق وتتبّع الكود الأصلي اللي بيعالج الـ redirect الوارد: CustomTabFlowActivity -> CustomTabFlowViewModel.f(Uri) -> BrowserFlowResultManager.a(Uri). في المسار ده كلّه ملقاش أي نقطة بتتحقق إن الـ state أو code أو token اللي جايين في الـ URI مربوطين بتدفق بدأه نفس الـ instance من التطبيق — مفيش مقارنة nonce/state، مفيش فحص PKCE verifier، ومفيش تحقق من هوية الـ caller. الطريقة ببساطة بتعيد نشر أي Uri بتوصّل له كأنه "flow completed" لأي business logic مستمعة في اللحظة دي. النتيجة إن أي تطبيق أو صفحة ضارة تقدر تفتح الـ deep link ده بـ URI مفبرك، والتطبيق هيتعامل معاه كأنه نتيجة تدفق OAuth شرعي — وده بيفتح باب لاختطاف تدفق OAuth/SSO وربط حسابات بطرف تالت بشكل غير مصرح به.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أي تطبيق Android فيه OAuth/SSO مبني على المتصفح لازم تبدأ فحصك من الـ manifest: دوّر على Activities مكتوبة بـ android:exported="true" ومسجّلة كـ redirect target لـ custom schemes أو App Links. بعدها فكّك التطبيق وتتبّع مسار معالجة الـ Uri من الـ Activity للـ ViewModel للـ Manager، وافحص كل نقطة على الطريق: هل في مقارنة state/nonce؟ هل في PKCE verifier؟ هل في تحقق من هوية الـ caller؟ غياب أي واحدة من دول علامة قوية على ثغرة Insecure Authorization. نفس النمط بيتكرر في أي تطبيق بيعتمد على OAuth redirects — مش بس الهدف ده.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح إن معالجة الـ redirect لازم تتحقق إن الـ state أو nonce اللي راجع في الـ URI هو نفس اللي التطبيق ولّده وربطه بالتدفق اللي بدأه — مقارنة صارمة قبل ما تنشر أي نتيجة لأي business logic. كمان لازم يتفعّل PKCE مع تخزين الـ verifier في جلسة التدفق نفسها والتحقق منه عند الـ callback. الـ Activity نفسها لازم تبقى مش exported، أو لو لازمة exported يبقى في permission مخصصة وفحص هوية الـ caller قبل معالجة الـ Uri. ويفضل الاعتماد على App Links مع autoVerify بدل custom schemes، مع التحقق الصارم من الـ host والـ path لكل redirect وارد.
